span.label: method
span.quote: Here we present a principled statistical framework for discerning and quantifying power-law behavior in empirical data.

span.label: power-law distributions in empirical data
span.quote: Power-law distributions occur in many situations of scientific interest and have significant consequences for our understanding of natural and man-made phenomena.

span.label: simulation
span.quote: We evaluate the effectiveness of the approach with tests on synthetic data and give critical comparisons to previous approaches.

span.label: Known sampling biases in several of the reanalysed data sets were left uncorrected.
span.quote: We have not attempted to correct any biases in our analysis.

span.label: Many of the reanalysed data sets are partial samples of larger populations.
span.quote: Many of these data sets are only subsets of much larger entities (such as the web sites, which are only a small fraction of the entire web).

span.label: The framework is presented only for the power law; no extension to other distributional forms is given.
span.quote: In principle, they could also be extended to other, non-power-law distributions as well, although we have not given such an extension here.

span.label: The procedure often cannot separate power-law from log-normal behaviour.
span.quote: In general, we find that it is extremely difficult to tell the difference between log-normal and power-law behavior.

span.label: Two model forms indistinguishable on the observed data can give enormously different extrapolations into the tail, which is where such fits are usually applied.
span.quote: if we wish to extrapolate a fitted distribution far into its tail, to predict, for example, the frequencies of large but rare events like major earthquakes or meteor impacts, then conclusions based on different fitted forms can differ enormously even if the forms are indistinguishable in the domain covered by the actual data.

span.label: Seven of the twenty-four data sets previously conjectured to be power laws are firmly ruled out.
span.quote: The p-values in Table 6.1 indicate that 17 of the 24 data sets are consistent with a power-law distribution. The remaining seven data sets all have p-values small enough that the power-law model can be firmly ruled out.

span.label: The range fitted is chosen, and that choice controls how much data the test sees.

span.label: Errors run in both directions on small samples: a power law can look like a good fit to non-power-law data, and true power laws cannot be separated from alternatives.
span.quote: it is difficult to rule out alternative fits to such data, even when they are truly power-law distributed, and conversely the power-law form may appear to be a good fit even when the data are drawn from a non-power-law distribution.
